title: Some and any
description: Say how much with du, de la, de l’ and des, and know when they become de.

guide.summary: Du, de la, de l’ and des say “some”: an amount you do not count. Learn the four forms, then learn the places where they shrink to de or give way to le, la, les.

sections.title: Which one: du, de la, de l’ or des?
sections.text: French cannot leave a noun bare. Where English says “I drink milk”, French marks the amount with a partitive article.

rows: de la soupe, de la viande

steps: Ask how much: an unspecified amount, not one whole thing? Then you need a partitive.
Find the noun’s gender and number.
Check its first letter: a vowel or a silent h takes the elided form, whatever the gender.

examples.fr: Le matin, je bois du café.
examples.en: In the morning I drink coffee.

watch: English often uses no word at all: “I drink milk” is je bois du lait, never je bois lait.
Only the noun decides the gender: du jus d’orange stays masculine because jus is.
Du and de la never stand in front of a vowel sound.

sections.title: The thing in general, or some of it?
sections.text: Aimer, adorer, détester and préférer talk about the thing in general: they take le, la, l’, les, even in a negative sentence. Manger, boire, acheter, prendre and vouloir talk about an amount, so they take the partitive.
steps: Look at the verb before you look at the noun.
Liking, loving, hating, preferring: use the definite article.
Eating, drinking, buying, wanting: use the partitive.
A negation never changes what a verb of taste takes.

examples.fr: J’aime le thé, mais je bois beaucoup de café.
examples.en: I like tea, but I drink a lot of coffee.

watch: Je n’aime pas de poisson is wrong: pas de denies an amount, and aimer is not about amounts.
The same noun changes article with the verb: il aime la salade, il mange de la salade.

sections.title: After ne…pas the partitive becomes de
sections.text: When a negation denies an amount, all four partitives collapse into de, shortened to d’ before a vowel or a silent h.

rows: je ne bois pas de café
elle ne mange pas de viande

steps: Check that the negation denies an amount, not an identity.
Replace the whole partitive with the single short word de: no gender, no number.
Drop its e before a vowel or a silent h.
Keep ne in writing, as n’ before a vowel.

examples.fr: Je ne bois pas de café le soir.
examples.en: I don’t drink coffee in the evening.

examples.fr: Il n’y a pas d’eau dans la bouteille.
examples.en: There is no water in the bottle.

watch: Pas du, pas de la and pas des do not exist when an amount is denied.
Speech drops ne, writing keeps it: je n’ai pas de frères.

sections.title: Why ce n’est pas du café keeps its article
sections.text: Être measures nothing: a negative sentence with être says what something is not. Nothing shrinks there, so the article stays whole.

rows: du, de la, de l’ stay
de, or d’ before a vowel

steps: Find the negated verb.
Être: keep exactly the article the positive sentence would have.
Any other verb denying an amount: reduce the article to de.

examples.fr: Ce n’est pas du café, c’est du thé.
Ce ne sont pas des pommes, ce sont des poires.

watch: Ce n’est pas de soupe is wrong: the sentence says what the food is, not how much of it there is.
For one thing say ce n’est pas, for several ce ne sont pas.

sections.title: After a quantity word: de and nothing else
sections.text: A word that measures, whether an adverb of quantity or a container, is followed by de with no article at all.
steps: Spot the measuring word in front of the noun.
Put de after it and drop the article completely.
Shorten de to d’ before a vowel or a silent h.

examples.fr: Il met trop de sel dans la soupe.
examples.en: He puts too much salt in the soup.

examples.fr: Je voudrais une bouteille de lait.
examples.en: I would like a bottle of milk.

watch: Beaucoup du café is wrong: a quantity word leaves no article behind.
Two nouns never touch: une bouteille lait needs the link word.

sections.title: Faire + activity: faire du sport
sections.text: Doing a sport, an instrument or a hobby uses faire plus a partitive. The gender and the first letter of the activity decide which one.

rows: faire du sport, faire du vélo, faire du yoga
to do sport, to cycle, to do yoga
faire de la musique, faire de la danse, faire de la natation
to play music, to dance, to swim

steps: Keep faire and put the activity straight after it.
Pick the partitive that matches the activity’s gender and first letter.
In a negative sentence faire behaves like any other verb: the partitive becomes de.

examples.fr: Le samedi, je fais du sport.
Ma sœur fait de la musique.
Nous ne faisons pas de vélo le dimanche.

watch: Faire le sport is not said: with faire the activity takes a partitive.
Elle fait de danse is wrong: only a negation or a quantity word reduces the article to de.

steps: Check the sentence is positive and has no quantity word in front of the noun.
Find the noun’s gender: le before it means masculine, la means feminine.
Take that row of the table; words added after the noun do not change it.
Look at the number first: a plural noun takes one single form for both genders.
For a singular noun, check its first letter: a vowel or a silent h gives the elided form.
Remember that h is usually silent, so the word counts as beginning with a vowel.
Check what the negation denies: an amount, not what something is.
Replace the whole partitive with the one short word, whatever the gender and number.
Drop its e before a vowel or a silent h, and keep ne (n’) in writing.
Find the negated verb.
If it is être, keep the article the positive sentence would use: nothing is reduced.
Then choose that article by the noun’s gender, number and first letter.
Spot the quantity word or container word before the noun.
Follow it with de and no article at all.
Shorten de before a vowel or a silent h.
Read the verb: does it express taste, or an amount taken?
A verb of taste takes the definite article, in positive and negative sentences alike.
Then match that article to the noun’s gender, number and first letter.
Check it is faire plus an activity, in a positive sentence.
Choose the partitive from the activity’s gender and first letter.
If the sentence is negative, reduce the article like any ordinary verb.

exercises.hint: An unspecified amount of coffee. Is café masculine or feminine?
exercises.feedback: Café is masculine and does not begin with a vowel.
exercises.explanation: For some of a masculine noun, use du: je bois du café.

mistakes.why: De la is the feminine form. Le café is masculine, so it takes the masculine partitive.
De l’ appears only before a vowel or a silent h. Café begins with the consonant c.

exercises.hint: Some soup, not a whole soup. What is the gender of soupe?
exercises.feedback: Soupe is feminine and singular.
exercises.explanation: For some of a feminine noun, use de la: de la soupe.

mistakes.why: Du is the masculine form. Soupe is feminine, la soupe, so it needs the feminine partitive.
Des is for a plural noun. Soupe here is one singular noun.

exercises.source: Nous achetons ____ pain à la boulangerie.
exercises.hint: Some bread. What is the gender of pain?
exercises.feedback: Pain is masculine.
exercises.explanation: Le pain is masculine, so some bread is du pain.

mistakes.why: That is the feminine form, but le pain is masculine.
The elided form stands only before a vowel or a silent h. Pain begins with p.
Des is plural. Pain here is one singular noun, not several loaves.
Bare de follows a negation or a quantity word. This sentence is positive and has neither.

exercises.hint: English has no article here, but French needs one for an amount of milk.
exercises.feedback: Boire takes the partitive, and lait is masculine.
exercises.explanation: Milk here is an unspecified amount, so French uses du: je bois du lait.

mistakes.why: English needs no word before milk, but French cannot leave the noun bare: an amount always takes an article.
Je bois le lait means the milk, one particular milk. Here milk is an unspecified amount.
That is the feminine form, and le lait is masculine.
Bare de follows a negation or a quantity word, and this sentence has neither.

exercises.source: Il boit de la jus d’orange.
exercises.hint: What is the gender of jus?
exercises.feedback: Jus is not feminine.
exercises.explanation: Le jus is masculine, so some juice is du jus. The d’orange part does not change the gender.

answers: Il boit de la jus d’orange.
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Le jus is masculine, so the feminine article in front of it is the error.
That says he drinks the juice, one particular one. The sentence is about an unspecified amount.
Bare de follows a negation or a quantity word, and there is neither here.
Des would count several separate juices. Here it is an amount of one drink.

exercises.instruction: Build the French sentence. Leave any extra tiles unused.
exercises.hint: Some cheese: what is the gender of fromage? One tile stays unused.
exercises.feedback: Fromage is masculine. Pick the partitive that matches.
exercises.explanation: Fromage is masculine, so some cheese is du fromage.

mistakes.why: That tile is the feminine article, and le fromage is masculine.
English says “we eat cheese” with no word before it; French always puts an article in front of the noun.

exercises.hint: Eau begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Before a vowel, du and de la become one form.
exercises.explanation: Before a vowel or silent h, both du and de la become de l’: de l’eau.

mistakes.why: De la is the feminine form used before a consonant. Eau begins with a vowel, so the a cannot stay.
Du is masculine and l’eau is feminine. Du could not stand before a vowel either.

exercises.hint: Œufs is plural.
exercises.feedback: Du and de la are only for singular nouns.
exercises.explanation: For some of a plural noun, use des: des œufs.

mistakes.why: Du is for a singular masculine noun. Œufs is plural.
De la is for a singular feminine noun. Œufs is plural, and masculine as well.

exercises.instruction: Write du, de la, de l’ or des.
exercises.hint: The h in huile is silent.
exercises.feedback: Huile sounds as if it begins with a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Huile has a silent h, so the partitive is de l’: de l’huile.

mistakes.why: De la stands before a consonant sound. The h of huile is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound.
Du is masculine; l’huile is feminine, and du never stands before a vowel sound anyway.
Des is plural. Huile here is one uncountable liquid.
Bare de follows a negation or a quantity word. This sentence is positive and has neither.

exercises.source: Do you want some water? (to a friend)
answers: Est-ce que tu veux de l’eau ?
exercises.hint: Some water: eau begins with a vowel. To a friend, use tu.
exercises.feedback: Check the partitive before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Eau begins with a vowel, so some water is de l’eau. The question can use intonation, est-ce que or inversion.

alternatives.message: That is correct French, but it means a little water. Here, practise the partitive for some water.
That is correct, but it means would you like. Do you want is tu veux.

mistakes.why: De la keeps its a only before a consonant sound, and eau begins with a vowel.
Du is masculine and l’eau is feminine; du cannot sit before a vowel either.
That is the vous form, for a stranger or several people. The question is put to a friend.
That asks for the water, one particular water. The English asks for an unspecified amount.

exercises.instruction: Replace lait with eau and change the article.
exercises.hint: The new noun begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Du cannot stand before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Eau begins with a vowel, so du becomes de l’: je bois de l’eau.

mistakes.why: Nothing has changed: the task is to put the new noun in and adapt its article.
Du is masculine, l’eau is feminine, and du cannot stand before a vowel.
That form fits a feminine noun beginning with a consonant; eau begins with a vowel.
That means the water, one particular one. The sentence is about an unspecified amount.

exercises.hint: Pommes is plural.
exercises.feedback: Du is only for a singular masculine noun.
exercises.explanation: Pommes is plural, so the partitive is des: des pommes.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Du is singular and masculine, while pommes is plural.
That is a singular feminine article in front of a plural noun.
Bare de follows a negation or a quantity word, and this sentence has neither.
Les pommes means the apples, particular ones. He is buying an unspecified quantity.

exercises.source: Je ne bois pas ____ café le soir.
exercises.hint: After ne…pas, the partitive article changes.
exercises.feedback: The sentence is negative.
exercises.explanation: After a negation, du, de la and des become de: je ne bois pas de café.

mistakes.why: Du belongs in a positive sentence. Here ne…pas denies the amount, so the partitive shrinks.
That is a positive-sentence form, and it is feminine, while le café is masculine.

exercises.source: Il n’y a pas ____ eau dans la bouteille.
exercises.hint: Negative sentence, and eau begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: After ne…pas, the partitive becomes one short word.
exercises.explanation: After a negation, de l’ becomes de, and de becomes d’ before a vowel: pas d’eau.

mistakes.why: That is the form for a positive sentence. After ne…pas the article is reduced.
That is a positive-sentence form too, and it could not stand before a vowel anyway.

exercises.hint: Negative sentence, and enfants begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Des becomes a short form after ne…pas.
exercises.explanation: After a negation, des becomes de, and de becomes d’ before a vowel: pas d’enfants.

mistakes.why: The full form is kept before a consonant. Enfants begins with a vowel, so the e goes.
Des belongs in the positive sentence. A negation of quantity replaces the plural article.
That is a singular positive-sentence form, and enfants is plural.

answers: Elle ne mange pas de viande.
exercises.hint: Put ne…pas around the verb and look at the article.
exercises.feedback: The article changes in a negative sentence.
exercises.explanation: Ne…pas goes around mange, and de la becomes de: elle ne mange pas de viande.

answers: Elle ne mange pas de la viande.
mistakes.why: The negation is added but the article is not touched. After ne…pas no gender form survives.

answers: Elle ne mange pas du viande.
mistakes.why: Du is masculine, la viande is feminine, and a positive-sentence article cannot follow pas.
That leaves out ne. Speech drops it, but written French keeps ne in front of the verb.

answers: Elle ne mange pas la viande.
mistakes.why: La viande names one particular meat. The sentence denies an amount, not a specific dish.

exercises.hint: Ne becomes n’ before ai, and the article changes.
exercises.feedback: Two things change: the negation and the article.
exercises.explanation: Ne becomes n’ before a vowel, and des becomes de after a negation: je n’ai pas de frères. Je n’ai pas de frère, in the singular, is just as correct.

answers: Je ne ai pas de frères.
mistakes.why: Ne cannot stay whole before a vowel: it loses its e and takes an apostrophe.
Des belongs in the positive sentence. After ne…pas the plural article is replaced.
That leaves out ne. Written French keeps it, joined to the verb as n’.

answers: Il n’y a pas de lait.

alternatives.answer: Il y a pas de lait.
alternatives.message: In speech the ne is often dropped, but written French keeps it: write n’…pas.

exercises.hint: Use il n’y a pas and think about the article after a negation.
exercises.feedback: After a negation, the partitive becomes one short word.
exercises.explanation: There is no milk is il n’y a pas de lait: after ne…pas, du becomes de.

answers: Il n’y a pas du lait.
mistakes.why: Du belongs in a positive sentence. After ne…pas the article is reduced to its short form.
French cannot leave the noun bare after pas: a short word still links them.
That says he has no milk. There is and there are are il y a.

answers: Il n’y a pas le lait.
mistakes.why: Le lait means the milk, one particular one. The sentence says there is none at all.

exercises.source: Je ne veux pas du sucre.
answers: Je ne veux pas de sucre.
exercises.hint: The sentence is negative.
exercises.feedback: Look at the word after pas.
exercises.explanation: After a negation, du becomes de: je ne veux pas de sucre.

answers: Je ne veux pas du sucre.
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Du belongs in a positive sentence; a negation of quantity replaces it.

answers: Je ne veux pas le sucre.
mistakes.why: Le sucre means the sugar, one particular lot of it. The sentence refuses any at all.
That deletes ne instead of fixing the article. Written French keeps ne before the verb.

exercises.instruction: Build the French sentence. Leave any extra tiles unused.
exercises.hint: The sentence is negative. One tile stays unused.
exercises.feedback: Du does not follow pas.
exercises.explanation: After ne…pas, du becomes de: il n’achète pas de vin.

mistakes.why: That tile is the positive-sentence article. The sentence is negative, so the article is reduced.
French does not leave the noun bare after pas: one short word still stands in front of it.

exercises.source: Ce n’est pas ____ café, c’est du thé.
exercises.hint: Is this negation about an amount, or about what the thing is?
exercises.feedback: With être, the article does not change.
exercises.explanation: Être is not a negation of quantity: ce n’est pas du café says what the drink is, so du stays.

mistakes.why: Bare de follows pas when an amount is denied. Here être says what the drink is, not how much there is.
That is de shortened before a vowel; café begins with a consonant, and this negation reduces nothing anyway.

exercises.source: Ce ne sont pas ____ pommes, ce sont des poires.
exercises.hint: The negation is on être, not on an amount.
exercises.feedback: Être keeps the full article.
exercises.explanation: After a negative form of être, des stays: ce ne sont pas des pommes.

mistakes.why: Bare de follows pas only when an amount is denied. Ce ne sont pas says what the fruit is, so the article stays whole.
That is the shortened form used before a vowel; pommes begins with a consonant, and nothing is reduced here.

exercises.instruction: Write du, de la or de l’.
exercises.source: Ce n’est pas ____ eau, c’est du vin blanc.
exercises.hint: After ce n’est pas, the article stays as it was.
exercises.feedback: This negation uses être, so the partitive keeps its full form.
exercises.explanation: With être the partitive does not shrink, and eau begins with a vowel: ce n’est pas de l’eau.

mistakes.why: Bare de follows pas when an amount is denied, but être only says what the liquid is.
That short form belongs after a negation of quantity. This negation is on être.
That form fits a feminine noun beginning with a consonant; eau begins with a vowel.
Du is masculine and l’eau is feminine.

exercises.source: Ce n’est pas de soupe, c’est de la sauce.
answers: Ce n’est pas de la soupe, c’est de la sauce.
exercises.hint: Which verb is negative here?
exercises.feedback: Être keeps the full partitive.
exercises.explanation: The negated verb is être, so de la does not become de: ce n’est pas de la soupe.

answers: Ce n’est pas de soupe, c’est de la sauce.
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Bare de after pas denies an amount, but être only says what the food is.

answers: Ce n’est pas du soupe, c’est de la sauce.
mistakes.why: Du is masculine and la soupe is feminine.

answers: Ce n’est pas de soupe, c’est de sauce.
mistakes.why: That strips the second article too. Être never reduces a partitive, so both nouns keep a full one.

answers: Ce n’est pas du jus, c’est du lait.
Ce n’est pas du jus c’est du lait.

alternatives.answer: C’est pas du jus, c’est du lait.
alternatives.message: In speech the ne is often dropped, but written French keeps it: write n’…pas.

exercises.hint: Use ce n’est pas and c’est. Does the article change with être?
exercises.feedback: With être, the partitive keeps its full form.
exercises.explanation: Ce n’est pas du jus keeps du, because être is not a negation of quantity. Both nouns are masculine.

answers: Ce n’est pas de jus, c’est du lait.
mistakes.why: Bare de after pas denies an amount; here the negation is on être, which says what the drink is.

answers: Ce n’est pas de la jus, c’est du lait.
mistakes.why: Le jus is masculine, so a feminine article does not fit it.

answers: Il n’est pas du jus, c’est du lait.
mistakes.why: To say what something is, French uses ce, not il.

answers: Ce n’est pas jus, c’est lait.
mistakes.why: English can leave both nouns bare; French puts an article in front of each one.

exercises.instruction: Make it negative: change c’est to ce n’est pas. Keep the right article.
answers: Ce n’est pas de la crème.
exercises.hint: Think about which verb is negative.
exercises.feedback: With être the article does not become de.
exercises.explanation: Ce n’est pas de la crème keeps de la: être is not a negation of quantity.

mistakes.why: Bare de after pas denies an amount. Être says what the thing is, so the article keeps its full form.
That drops ne. Written French keeps ne before the verb, as n’ in front of a vowel.
Du is masculine and la crème is feminine.

answers: Ce ne sont pas de la crème.
mistakes.why: Ce ne sont pas is the plural form, for several things. Crème here is one singular noun.

exercises.source: Il y a beaucoup ____ monde ici.
exercises.hint: Beaucoup is a word of quantity.
exercises.feedback: After a quantity, the article disappears.
exercises.explanation: After beaucoup, use de alone: beaucoup de monde.

mistakes.why: Du is the article you use when nothing measures the noun. Beaucoup measures it, so the article goes.
Des is a plural article; monde is singular here, and a quantity word takes no article at all.

exercises.hint: Un verre is a quantity, and eau begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: After a quantity, only de remains, shortened before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: After un verre, use de alone, and de becomes d’ before a vowel: un verre d’eau.

mistakes.why: That full article is for a noun with nothing in front of it. Un verre measures the water, so the article goes.
That is the full feminine article. A container word leaves only the short link, and eau begins with a vowel.

exercises.source: Il met trop ____ sel dans la soupe.
exercises.hint: Trop is a word of quantity.
exercises.feedback: After trop, no article follows.
exercises.explanation: After trop, use de alone: trop de sel.

mistakes.why: Du is for a noun with no quantity word before it. Trop is one, so the article disappears.
That is feminine and le sel is masculine; after trop no gender form survives anyway.
The e is dropped only before a vowel or a silent h, and sel begins with s.
Des is plural, and a quantity word takes no article at all.

exercises.source: Nous avons assez ____ argent pour le voyage.
exercises.hint: Assez is a word of quantity, and argent begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: After assez, only de remains.
exercises.explanation: After assez, use de alone, shortened to d’ before a vowel: assez d’argent.

mistakes.why: The full form stands before a consonant. Argent begins with a vowel, so the e is dropped.
That full article is for a noun with nothing in front of it. Assez measures the money, so the article goes.
Du is the masculine article for a noun with no quantity word, and it never stands before a vowel.
Des is plural; argent is singular, and a quantity word takes no article.

exercises.source: I would like a bottle of milk.
answers: Je voudrais une bouteille de lait.
exercises.hint: Une bouteille is a quantity.
exercises.feedback: After a container word, use de alone.
exercises.explanation: After a quantity like une bouteille, use de alone: une bouteille de lait.

answers: Je voudrais une bouteille du lait.
mistakes.why: Du is the article for a noun with nothing in front of it. After a container word only the short link stays.
A container and its content are always linked by a short word; two nouns cannot touch.

answers: Je voudrais un bouteille de lait.
mistakes.why: Bouteille is feminine, so the word for one in front of it must be feminine too.

answers: Je veux une bouteille de lait.
mistakes.why: Je veux is a blunt “I want”. “I would like” is the polite conditional form.

exercises.hint: Beaucoup is a word of quantity.
exercises.feedback: After beaucoup, du does not appear.
exercises.explanation: After beaucoup, use de alone: beaucoup de café.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Beaucoup measures the coffee, so no article follows it.

answers: Elle boit beaucoup de la café.
mistakes.why: That keeps a feminine article in front of a masculine noun, and a quantity word takes no article at all.
That deletes beaucoup instead of fixing what follows it. The sentence should keep its quantity word.
The e is dropped only before a vowel or a silent h, and café begins with c.

exercises.instruction: Add un peu to say a little.
answers: Je prends un peu de sucre.
exercises.hint: Un peu is a quantity, so the article changes.
exercises.feedback: After un peu, du disappears.
exercises.explanation: After un peu, use de alone: je prends un peu de sucre.

answers: Je prends un peu du sucre.
mistakes.why: The quantity word is added but the article is kept. A quantity word leaves no article behind.

answers: Je prends un peu de la sucre.
mistakes.why: Le sucre is masculine, and after a quantity word no gender form survives either.

answers: Je prends du sucre un peu.
mistakes.why: Un peu belongs in front of the noun it measures, not at the end of the sentence.

exercises.instruction: Build the French sentence. Leave any extra tiles unused.
exercises.source: There is a lot of snow.
answers: Il y a beaucoup de neige.
exercises.hint: Beaucoup is a quantity. One tile stays unused.
exercises.feedback: After beaucoup, only de follows.
exercises.explanation: After beaucoup, use de alone: beaucoup de neige.

answers: Il y a beaucoup de la neige.
mistakes.why: After a quantity word the article is dropped; only the short link stays.

answers: Il y a de la neige.
mistakes.why: That says there is snow but loses “a lot of”. The quantity tile has to be used.
A quantity word is joined to its noun by a short word; the two cannot sit side by side.

exercises.hint: Aimer talks about something in general.
exercises.feedback: Verbs of liking do not take the partitive.
exercises.explanation: Aimer takes the definite article for the thing in general: j’aime le café noir.

mistakes.why: Du is for an amount you drink. Aimer is about coffee in general, so it takes the definite article.
Bare de follows a negation or a quantity word, and there is neither here.

exercises.hint: Adorer works like aimer.
exercises.feedback: Verbs of liking take the definite article.
exercises.explanation: Adorer takes the definite article, and frites is plural: les frites.

mistakes.why: Des is the partitive, for an amount eaten. Adorer is about chips in general, so it takes the definite plural article.
Bare de follows a negation or a quantity word, and neither appears here.

exercises.hint: Aimer keeps its article even in a negative sentence.
exercises.feedback: Pas de is for amounts. Aimer is about fish in general.
exercises.explanation: Aimer takes the definite article, and a negation does not change it: je n’aime pas le poisson.

exercises.hint: Aimer and manger do not take the same article.

answers: Il aime du fromage, alors il mange le fromage.
